common_name: Brison Blackberry (Texas A&M Blackland-Clay Thorny Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted transplants January-March in zone 9; thorny and erect, so wear heavy gloves. Site it with excellent air movement and avoid overhead irrigation, since it is prone to rosette (double blossom) fungal disease in humid conditions.

directions: Brison is a thorny, erect-to-semi-erect blackberry released by Texas A&M University in 1977 and long favored across the western Gulf South for its reliable performance on heavy blackland clay soils where many other cultivars struggle. Fruit is firmer and sweeter than the older Texas standard Brazos, and plants are early-bearing and consistently productive. Its main drawback is susceptibility to rosette (double blossom), so prune out any distorted, witches'-broom-like growth promptly and keep plantings open and well-ventilated. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto a simple trellis for easier picking around the thorns.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Blackberry Varieties for Louisiana

common_name: Black Gem Blackberry (APF-205T Thornless Primocane University of Arkansas Release)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tissue-culture transplants in late winter or early spring; thornless and primocane-fruiting, giving a floricane crop in early summer and a second primocane crop from late summer into fall.

directions: Bred by John R. Clark at the University of Arkansas as selection APF-205T, patented and introduced in 2017 and later marketed as Stark Black Gem, this thornless, upright blackberry fruits on both second-year floricanes and current-season primocanes. Berries are notably sweet, with 11-12% soluble solids and lower acidity than most blackberries, giving it a dessert-quality flavor, and mature plants have been reported to yield 11-15 pounds of fruit per season. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and provide a simple trellis for the vigorous canes. Prune spent floricanes to the ground after the early crop and tip primocanes in midsummer to encourage lateral branching for the fall harvest.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Zodiac Blackberry (Thornless Trailing Machine-Harvest Processing Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 6-8 feet apart in rows at least 8-10 feet apart, and install a sturdy multi-wire trellis since the long trailing canes will not support themselves.

directions: Zodiac is a thornless trailing blackberry from the USDA-ARS/Oregon State cooperative breeding program in Corvallis, Oregon, bred from two thornless selections, ORDS 2707-1 and ORDS 2785-2. It produces high, early-to-midseason yields of small-to-medium, glossy, conical berries with firm texture and a strong, aromatic, well-balanced sugar-acid flavor, and is bred primarily for machine harvest in commercial processing fields. Like other trailing types it needs vigorous training onto a multi-wire trellis and generous row spacing. Its Pacific Northwest breeding background means it is best suited to cooler-summer climates and will need trialing for heat and disease tolerance before relying on it in hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Corvallis, OR small fruit breeding program

common_name: Celestial Blackberry (Heat-Tolerant Thornless Semi-Erect USDA Release)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early spring, spacing 4-6 feet apart in rows at least 8 feet apart, and set up a two- or three-wire trellis since the semi-erect canes benefit from support once heavily loaded with fruit.

directions: Celestial, patented in 2023, is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry from the USDA-ARS/Oregon State cooperative program, bred from a cross between the thornless Eclipse and a thorny breeding selection carrying wild and cultivated Rubus germplasm from the southeastern United States. That Southeastern parentage gives Celestial noticeably better heat tolerance than most Oregon-bred blackberries. It yields heavily over a long mid-to-late-season harvest window, with small-to-medium, glossy, low-defect berries of excellent flavor. Canes are largely self-supporting but crop better on a simple trellis; remove fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and train in new primocanes for next year's crop.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Corvallis, OR small fruit breeding program

common_name: Everthornless Blackberry (Non-Reverting Thornless Cutleaf Trailing Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes on a sturdy trellis in early spring; the long trailing canes are vigorous and need firm tying and regular pruning to keep the planting contained.

directions: Everthornless, developed at the University of Illinois as an ex vitro somaclonal variant of the classic cutleaf Thornless Evergreen blackberry, was bred to fix a longstanding flaw in its parent: because Thornless Evergreen's thornlessness comes from a chimeral mutation confined to the outer cell layer, its root suckers frequently revert to thorny growth as plantings age. Everthornless carries the thornless trait through all cell layers, so its root suckers stay thornless too, making it a lower-maintenance option for replanting old Thornless Evergreen patches. It keeps the same deeply cut, fern-like foliage and produces good yields of well-flavored, mildly tart berries late in the season. Train the vigorous trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis, prune hard after harvest, and keep cane tips off the soil to prevent unwanted rooting.
